newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Rains bring relief to damaged S.Africa maize crop.
newsitem.headline: Rains bring relief to damaged S.Africa maize crop.

text.p: South Africa's maize industry welcomed soaking rains that began overnight and continued on Wednesday, saying the showers would for now arrest further damage to the drought-hit crop.

Experts said recent panic that the new crop will be sharply down on last year's bumper 9.5 million tonne harvest following hot and dry weather in the crucial growing months of January and February, had abated somewhat.
"The rain won't improve the crop but it will certaintly stabilise the crop," said Andre Ferreira, economist at the National Maize Producers Organisation (Nampo).

"There is definitely permanent damage to the crop but the rain will prohibit further deterioration," he told Reuters, declining to give an estimate of the size of the harvest in South Africa's most important agricultural commodity.
Nampo said late last month that scorching weather could cut the 1997 crop, due to be harvested from May, to between 7.0 and 7.8 million tonnes.
And it warned of a drop to below six million tonnes, forcing the country to import, if rain remained scarce.

Maize industry experts on Wednesday predicted a crop of between seven and 8.5 million tonnes, down on the U.S. Agriculture Department February estimate of 9.5 million. The first official South African crop estimate is due around March 20.

Dealers on South Africa's futures market said the brisk trade and high prices in maize contracts in February amid crop concerns had tapered off this week following rains late last week and on Wednesday.
"People were scared of the drought, so the market was overbought...But it is very quiet now that it is raining," said a trader at a leading bank.
More rain, continuing until the end of the weekend, was forecast for the maize belt by the Weather Services Corp.
It said temperatures were expected to be warm on Friday and Saturday, then cooling on Sunday.

On Wednesday July white maize contracts were bid at 648 rand a tonne and offered at 675 rand compared to a high in February of 690 rand. July yellow maize was bid at 610 and offered at 649 from a 670 rand high.
